views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the imminent Trump–Xi G20 dinner to seek a time-limited ceasefire that postpones the January 1, 2019 jump of List 3 from 10% to 25% and holds off any $267B List 4, without unilaterally rolling back our existing retaliation or locking in large purchase/structural commitments before the United States tables a matching, enforceable offer. Keep current tariffs in place as leverage, restate willingness to expand purchases and market access in principle, and refuse to accept permanent U.S. tariffs as the price of talks. Do not add new tariff or non-tariff measures in the next few days; further escalation now would likely trigger the remaining U.S. coverage and close the only live negotiating window.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 Sep), with the rate on ~$200B scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 Jan 2019 and an explicit threat of another ~$267B that would hit almost all remaining exports to the U.S. (timeline 2018-09-17/24; USTR 18 Sep). That is the +0.5 CHN anchor: major export exposure, FX pressure, and firm-level tech targeting. The April 16 ZTE denial order showed Washington can operationally shut a national champion; FCC/Huawei pressure and Lists 1–2 aimed at ICT, robotics, and Made in China 2025 compound the technology risk. The yuan had already shed ~9% vs the dollar from April, the Shanghai Composite was in a bear market (~23% off the January peak by late August; SSE near 2,729 by 20 Sep), Q3 GDP eased to ~6.6%, surveyed urban unemployment ticked to 5.0% in August, and industrial losses were widening — trade-war expectations plus deleveraging, not a financial-stability break. Exports still grew earlier in the year and U.S. goods imports from China remained large into Oct–Nov (IMPCH $52.1B then $46.3B), so the export model is strained, not broken. Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. The May 19 joint statement (China to “significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin “on hold”) collapsed ten days later when Washington proceeded with the $50B tariffs — so premature purchase commitments without a tariff pause are a trap. China already matched the $50B and answered List 3 with 5–10% on ~$60B; remaining U.S. goods to tax are limited, while List 4 would be far more damaging to us. APEC produced no communiqué, Lighthizer said China has not changed “unfair” practices, Pence said strategy will not change until Beijing does, and Washington dismissed the 142-point list as lacking timetable and enforcement. At the same time, the Nov 1 phone call set a G20 meeting, back-channel talks resumed, and U.S. officials (Kudlow, NYT 27 Nov) were openly discussing a truce that delays the 25% hike because of market gyrations, rising rates, and GM layoffs. That is leverage, not a reason to fold. Unilateral rollback or concede_purchases would read as weakness at home and give hardliners a cheap win; further retaliation now would likely be answered with List 4. The disciplined move is to negotiate a pause and keep powder dry.
key_factors: US Section 301 already covers ~$250B; List 3 set to rise from 10% to 25% on 1 Jan 2019
Trump threat of additional ~$267B would cover nearly all remaining China-to-US goods
ZTE denial order and targeting of ICT/Made in China 2025 raise tech-sovereignty risk
Yuan ~9% weaker since April; A-share bear market; Q3 growth ~6.6%; urban jobless 5.0%
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed within 10 days when US proceeded with $50B tariffs
G20 Trump-Xi dinner is immediate; US side signaling possible delay of the 25% hike
China already retaliated ($3B + $50B + ~$60B); little room to escalate without inviting List 4
142-point offer rejected by USTR/Kudlow as lacking enforcement — do not over-concede before a matching US pause

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US goods imports from China still $52.1B in Oct 2018 then $46.3B in Nov — large volumes, some post-List-3 pullback, not a collapse.
Nominal broad USD index 116.83 on 2018-11-28, +4.5% over the window — dollar strength adds CNY/export pressure.

Trump may seek a G20 truce delaying the Jan 1 rise to 25% and holding off $267B more; Kudlow: good possibility of a deal, else happy to stand on tariffs. China reluctant to accept permanent US tariffs as weakness; 142-point list dismissed.
List 3 duties set to rise to 25% at start of 2019; Trump threatened duties on $267B more, i.e. almost all remaining China exports to the US.
Yuan down about 9% vs USD since April; Shanghai Composite in a bear market, about 23% off the January peak.
Q3 GDP ~6.6%; urban surveyed unemployment 5% in August (+0.2ppt); industrial losses up; SSE 2,729 as of 20 Sep; trade war weakening demand and supply.

APEC failed to produce a communiqué; Lighthizer: China has not altered unfair practices; Pence: strategy will not change; Chinese Washington trip cancelled; Xi opening-up remarks lacked concrete White House concessions.
